items.summary: The geometric characterization of masonry structures with incomplete or degraded surfaces remains a critical challenge in building rehabilitation, structural assessment, and BIM-based documentation. This study presents an automated computational framework for reconstructing the original geometry of partially collapsed masonry walls from Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) data, providing quantitatively defined uncertainty bounds to support informed decision-making in heritage conservation and the built environment. The proposed methodology integrates three complementary analytical components: i) automated wall thickness extraction based on PCA-driven point cloud segmentation combined with robust percentile statistics; ii) wall trajectory reconstruction through the identification of polygonal configurations and structural discontinuities between segments; and iii) slope profile detection using local gradient analysis to characterize wall batter angles. The entire workflow is implemented in Python within Jupyter Notebooks, ensuring transparency, reproducibility, and compliance with FAIR principles. Material characterization, informed by archaeological evidence and geotechnical parameters, enables the estimation of structural height through a limit equilibrium approach. A key contribution of this research is the Best-Fit Model Profile (BFMP) methodology for uncertainty quantification, which derives internal geometric references directly from the point cloud data. This approach allows for a systematic evaluation of preservation states and construction variability without reliance on external ground-truth measurements. Structural height estimation incorporates geotechnical and material parameters, whose influence is assessed through a sensitivity analysis, while the reported height interval propagates the thickness variability . Validation on a prehistoric masonry structure demonstrates the framework’s ability to transform ambiguous survey data into parametric, BIM-ready outputs with explicit uncertainty limits. Compared to traditional CAD-based reconstruction workflows, the proposed approach significantly reduces subjective interpretation while enhancing geometric reliability and analytical transparency
items.title: Automated geometric reconstruction of degraded prehistoric masonry from TLS data: reproducible workflow and synthetic benchmark (Valencina de la Concepción)

items.summary: Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11-seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision-language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918-1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years.
items.title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps

items.summary: EXTERNAL QIGONG AND HUMAN THERMAL RADIATION PATTERNS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating whether thermographic differences observed during culturally defined qigong and matched neutral tasks can be distinguished from ordinary human thermoregulation, environmental exchange and measurement bias. The governing three-coupling is infrared thermal imaging x physiological regulation x heat-transfer models. The research treats “external qi” as a cultural and experimental task label, not an established physical energy carrier. The scientific core separates raw infrared radiance from inferred skin temperature and estimated heat flux. It develops emissivity and reflected-wall correction, blackbody calibration, spectral detector response, conduction and perfusion bioheat models, convection, evaporation, respiration-related temperature patterns, posture and muscular activity. The original candidate bulk heat equation is explicitly refined by separating volumetric tissue transport from surface heat-transfer boundary conditions. The principal proposed test uses concealed task assignments, matched breathing/movement/clothing, phantom references, negative-control regions and conventional physics-first rivals. Thirty physically distinct mathematical plates document governing relationships, units, assumptions, identifiability, masked falsifiers and chapter links. Eighty-two independent research chapters contain 410 single-page investigations. The true center of the monograph is its 200 one-page Research Gates, each posing a falsifiable question in bold deep-navy typography and asking what an independent successor must measure, challenge, disprove or preserve. Thirty-three differentiated Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments, error-correction artifacts, negative-result protocols and reproducibility tools. The DOI registry separates three STARLI author mother volumes from eleven externally published methodological or conventional-science references on infrared thermography, emissivity, classical bioheat and research design. Bibliographic sources constrain methods; they do not validate extraordinary qigong mechanisms. Every integrated experiment is prospective. Ethical authorization and independent scientific review would be required before future human-observation research. items.summary: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target's own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.
items.title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

items.summary: On million-node graphs, the memory wall arrives before the compute wall: a GNN that never fits in VRAM cannot deliver the all-node inference its accuracy promises. The standard remedy, pruning, has always been an accuracy tax - paid once and never refunded. DPR refuses this framing. Its central insight is that the mask that shrinks training can also scaffold recovery: one compact node set bounds both computations of graph learning, serving as the encoder's training graph and, at inference, as the anchor from which a sparse structure-aware decoder rebuilds every pruned node (double-layer sparsification). The order is inverted - prune for efficiency, then reconstruct for accuracy - and the tax is repaid: the deployed 30%-budget model trains in 1,450 MiB of peak memory on one 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating a same-GPU rerun of the edge-sparsification baseline DSpar by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory; against the same-protocol full-batch no-prune encoder the deployed point pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax for a 2.8x smaller training footprint. Pruning without reconstruction leaves the encoder at 0.378 within the same 40-epoch window (Fig. 4), and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE, giving up approx. 5.4 pp of test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB of peak training memory; extended variants (long-range context, external text features, a CAN-bus application) are reported as extensions and do not compete with the deployed method, and the 41.8%-budget M4 point, scored on a coarsened super-node graph with its own split, is reported separately rather than compared with the original-node baselines. DPR thus turns aggressive node pruning from an accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator for VRAM-limited all-node inference.
items.title: Decoupled Prune-and-Reconstruct: Training on a Compact Core with Double-Layer Sparsification

items.summary: Video world models trained on large-scale robot data promise a safe and scalable approach for learning and evaluating policies that act in the physical world. However, they still struggle with long-horizon rollouts and out-of-distribution generalization, and they remain computationally demanding at inference time. Typically, video world models make predictions in the latent space of a reconstruction-trained autoencoder, which however is not directly optimized for dynamics modeling. On the other hand, world models designed for latent planning usually optimize latents to be predictable, but they forgo accurate prediction of observations in pixel space. In this paper, we show that it is possible to achieve the best of both worlds: a latent geometry optimized to make future prediction as simple as possible without sacrificing accurate prediction of future observations. More precisely, we find that temporal objectives for representation learning, paired with a past-conditioned decoder architecture, lead to consistent improvements in generative video world models at the same training budget. The gains include up to 5x cheaper inference, over 7x faster training, and 15-24% lower pixel and perceptual errors out of distribution and over long horizons. Our world models also agree more closely with real-world policy evaluation when using a vision-language model to judge task success from their pixel-space predictions. Overall, our study indicates that temporal predictability is an important design criterion for the latent space of video world models, and provides concrete guidance on how to incorporate it into the training of autoencoders.
items.title: Video World Models Need Predictable Latents

Each additional multigrid level halves both spatial dimensions using 2-by-2 block averaging. The initial implementation supports a single object slice, a single coherent shared probe, matching object/probe/detector sampling, and patch-based object sampling. Both object and probe are updated on every minibatch. Setup validates the supported configuration, multigrid depth, and initial guesses, including the requirement for nonzero amplitude at every object pixel. The default AUTO selects full-object sampling when the propagation distance is finite and both probe dimensions strictly exceed 80% of the corresponding object dimensions on the probe pixel grid. Set PATCH to explicitly select patch extraction and placement. Added periodic shifting of complete object slices, followed by a fixed center crop or zero-padding to match the probe shape. Fourier, bilinear, and nearest interpolation are supported, with matching additive adjoints. Features crossing an object boundary wrap to the opposite side. items.summary: Human observers can encounter representations of the same relational contribution history yet form different beliefs about its significance and trustworthiness. This third paper in a coordinated research programme investigates cognitive processes between the structural availability of evidence and an observer’s assessment of a person, claim, or contribution. Its proposed analytic objects are selective attention, evidence encoding, reconstructive memory, attribution, interpretive schemas, belief revision, epistemic vigilance, and behavioral reliance. The inquiry distinguishes evidentiary accessibility from cognitive encounter, subjective confidence from justified assessment, and expressed trust from risk-bearing cooperation. Prior work in attention, working memory, judgment under uncertainty, epistemic vigilance, and trust in automation motivates a provisional sequential-kernel architecture; that architecture remains a research proposal rather than a validated general cognitive model. AI-mediated information environments supply a historically relevant application, without defining the paper’s full scope. This working draft contains all ten planned sections, covering cognitive interfaces, selective attention, memory-based trajectory reconstruction, contribution attribution, proposition-specific belief revision, testimony evaluation, behavioral reliance, empirical designs with explicit identification boundaries, and a synthesis of conditional theoretical findings. It reports no original empirical results.
items.title: Cognitive Mediation of Relational Evidence: An Investigation of Epistemic Judgment and Reliance

items.summary: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
items.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex tasks, with multi-agent systems seeking further performance gains through specialization and collaboration. However, distributing work across agents does not automatically yield complementary contributions, and inter-agent dependencies can turn local errors into task failure. To address these challenges, we propose AutoSwarm, a multi-agent framework for collaborative problem solving. Collaboration formation jointly defines responsibility boundaries and conditions for acceptance and downstream use, grounding capability allocation in contributions that other agents can assess and integrate toward a shared objective. Execution coordination couples agents' local progress through a shared state, using dependencies and supervisory relationships to govern agent activation, result handoffs, and integration while adapting subsequent actions to review feedback and emerging blockers. Experiments spanning long-horizon programming, interactive planning, and professional financial analysis demonstrate AutoSwarm's advantages over single-agent baselines and existing multi-agent frameworks. Source code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/AutoSwarm.
items.title: AutoSwarm: Automating Agent Swarms

items.summary: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.
items.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents

In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. items.summary: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.
items.title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on role-specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi-Agent System Optimization through the joint adaptation of prompts and model assignments. UniMASO evaluates candidate updates through local, downstream, and global feedback, using cost-aware Pareto search to retain useful quality-cost trade-offs. Topology-aware co-evolution then coordinates these updates according to agent roles and dependencies. Cross-level trajectory memory further supplies historical successes and failures to guide subsequent optimization. Experiments on five benchmarks and five execution topologies show that UniMASO achieves competitive task performance at substantially lower deployment cost than the strongest homogeneous configurations. Under centralized execution, it improves the average score from 69.79 to 70.40 while reducing token-weighted deployment cost by 85.2% relative to DeepSeek-V4-Pro with MASPO. These results support joint prompt-model adaptation as an effective approach to efficient multi-agent collaboration. The code is available at https://github.com/Achilles008/UniMASO_main.
items.title: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
items.title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

items.summary: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) has become the dominant paradigm in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), motivating extensive study of what privileged information should be made available to the critic during training. While prior work has examined the role of global state in fully cooperative settings, the design of centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork - in which dynamically varying set of learning agents must coordinate with an arbitrary set of uncontrolled teammates drawn from an unknown distribution - remains poorly understood. We study this question by comparing two natural classes of advantage estimators: controlled history estimators, which condition only on the observation and action histories of the learner's own agents, and joint history estimators, which additionally condition on the histories of the uncontrolled teammates. We prove that both estimators are unbiased and characterize the conditions under which the joint history estimate attains strictly lower variance than its controlled counterpart. Empirically, joint history critics match or outperform controlled history critics across a range of NAHT tasks, yielding improved sample efficiency and final returns. Together, these results provide both a theoretical justification and an empirical recommendation for incorporating uncontrolled agent histories into centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork.
items.title: Centralized Critics for N-Agent Ad Hoc Teamwork

items.summary: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.
items.title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking

items.summary: EXTERNAL QIGONG AND HUMAN THERMAL RADIATION PATTERNS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating whether thermographic differences observed during culturally defined qigong and matched neutral tasks can be distinguished from ordinary human thermoregulation, environmental exchange and measurement bias. It develops emissivity and reflected-wall correction, blackbody calibration, spectral detector response, conduction and perfusion bioheat models, convection, evaporation, respiration-related temperature patterns, posture and muscular activity. Thirty physically distinct mathematical plates document governing relationships, units, assumptions, identifiability, masked falsifiers and chapter links. items.summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.
items.title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
items.title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.
items.title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: The geometric characterization of masonry structures with incomplete or degraded surfaces remains a critical challenge in building rehabilitation, structural assessment, and BIM-based documentation. This study presents an automated computational framework for reconstructing the original geometry of partially collapsed masonry walls from Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) data, providing quantitatively defined uncertainty bounds to support informed decision-making in heritage conservation and the built environment. The proposed methodology integrates three complementary analytical components: i) automated wall thickness extraction based on PCA-driven point cloud segmentation combined with robust percentile statistics; ii) wall trajectory reconstruction through the identification of polygonal configurations and structural discontinuities between segments; and iii) slope profile detection using local gradient analysis to characterize wall batter angles. The entire workflow is implemented in Python within Jupyter Notebooks, ensuring transparency, reproducibility, and compliance with FAIR principles. Material characterization, informed by archaeological evidence and geotechnical parameters, enables the estimation of structural height through a limit equilibrium approach. A key contribution of this research is the Best-Fit Model Profile (BFMP) methodology for uncertainty quantification, which derives internal geometric references directly from the point cloud data. This approach allows for a systematic evaluation of preservation states and construction variability without reliance on external ground-truth measurements. Structural height estimation incorporates geotechnical and material parameters, whose influence is assessed through a sensitivity analysis, while the reported height interval propagates the thickness variability . Validation on a prehistoric masonry structure demonstrates the framework’s ability to transform ambiguous survey data into parametric, BIM-ready outputs with explicit uncertainty limits. Compared to traditional CAD-based reconstruction workflows, the proposed approach significantly reduces subjective interpretation while enhancing geometric reliability and analytical transparency
items.title: Automated geometric reconstruction of degraded prehistoric masonry from TLS data: reproducible workflow and synthetic benchmark (Valencina de la Concepción)

items.summary: This replication package accompanies the manuscript  “How much coverage is enough? Spatially balanced partial-coverage thermal drone surveys for estimating ungulate density in forested landscapes.” The archive contains the R and Python code, georeferenced full-survey detections, observed partial-survey data, retrospective transect-intersection inputs, survey geometries, terrain inputs, compact simulation outputs and verification results needed to reproduce the drone-survey analyses. It includes workflows for reconstructing the reported full- and partial-coverage density estimates, statistical comparisons, perturbation analyses and post-processing simulation experiments. The original bootstrap analysis used 999 resamples without a recorded random seed. The archived workflow fixes the seed at 42; consequently, some bootstrap confidence limits and downstream test statistics differ slightly through Monte Carlo variation, while the reported conclusions remain unchanged. These differences are documented explicitly in the package. Raw survey videos, MOT annotation archives, raw camera-trap images and event-level camera-trap data are not redistributed. The archive instead contains the derived georeferenced detections and available transect-level inputs used by the reported drone analyses, which are actually required for replicating the results. The camera-trap comparison is represented by the area-level summary values used in the manuscript. Additional exclusions and their justification are documented in  docs/EXCLUSIONS.md . Reproduction instructions, a data dictionary, provenance information, validation results, software-environment details and a file-level checksum manifest are included.

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. items.summary: Continual graph learning (CGL) maintains models as graphs evolve without retraining from scratch, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods typically target either transductive or inductive settings and often store past subgraphs or require task identifiers at inference. We propose Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Continual Graph Learning (CoPE-CGL), a replay-free framework that uses a parameter-free structural prior, precomputed by multi-hop Laplacian smoothing, to anchor learning, memory, and inference. CoPE-CGL combines topology-infused bottleneck adaptation, community-level prototypes, and dynamic routing by majority vote over node-to-prototype matches. The default protocol assumes each test graph comes from one learned task; a node-level variant handles mixed-task graphs. Each task adds at most a constant amount of storage, with no past graph data retained. At equal storage and without task identifiers, CoPE-CGL matches the strongest replay baseline even when it receives true task identifiers: average performance (AP) is 95.17% and 95.72% versus 94.28% and 95.82% on Arxiv and CoraFull, respectively, with 5.9-14.0 times faster runtime and zero forgetting. Across four transductive and three inductive benchmarks and mixed streams, CoPE-CGL exceeds the second-best of up to eleven baselines by up to 1.41, 6.32, and 9.33 AP percentage points, respectively. It runs 1.3-7.9 times faster end-to-end than the most accurate competitor on each benchmark and scales to the largest benchmark graph. On graphs mixing two tasks, its node-level variant achieves the best AP among CGL methods. The design targets homophilic graphs with community structure.
items.title: CoPE-CGL: Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Replay-Free Continual Graph Learning

items.summary: Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research-proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared baselines.
items.title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration

items.summary: A staged, reproducible pipeline for VLT/MUSE narrow-field-mode integral-field data: raw-cube reduction, spectral extraction of a faint companion next to a much brighter primary star with six independent extraction schemes, and hydrogen-line accretion analysis with detection limits calibrated against empirical nulls from control positions processed identically to the object. Every stage emits a machine-readable quality-control document, and later stages read those documents rather than trusting assumptions; provenance (input cube, SHA-256 hashes, specification version, wavelength frame, flux unit) travels with the products. Research code under active development. This is the version used in Ramírez Reyes & Cáceres (in preparation).
items.title: MUSE accretion pipeline

items.summary: Web-connected sensing applications continuously generate multivariate time series with evolving behavioral categories, making Time Series Class-Incremental Learning (TSCIL) essential for adapting to new classes without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, preserving diverse and evolving class distributions under strict privacy and memory constraints remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often face a trade-off between retaining sufficient historical knowledge for accurate recognition and minimizing the memory required for continual adaptation. To address these limitations, we propose TRACE, a memory-efficient, replay-free framework that preserves class-specific knowledge through generative modeling rather than sample rehearsal. TRACE employs a compact, frozen temporal-spectral representation and lightweight class-specific autoencoders to capture complex intra-class variations. By independently preserving each class model, TRACE avoids recursive generation and catastrophic forgetting, while enabling direct classification through reconstruction-based scoring without retaining historical samples or large statistical matrices. Extensive experiments across five TSCIL benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE achieves competitive classification accuracy while reducing mean retained memory by approximately 98.26% compared with TS-ACL, the strongest evaluated analytical baseline, and achieving an approximately 33.43% relative improvement in accuracy on GrabMyo.
items.title: TRACE: Memory-Efficient Time Series Class-Incremental Learning via Temporal-Spectral Reconstruction

items.summary: Companion data deposit for the manuscript "Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation". This record contains the phenotype labels, genome feature matrices, train/test splits, trained model checkpoints, predicted proteomes, and figure and table source data underlying every script-generated display item in the manuscript and its supplementary material. The code that consumes it is on GitHub (links below); this record contains data only. CONTENTS - trait-prediction-data.zip (60 MB, 453 MB unpacked). All derived data: KOFAM, RAST and GapMind feature matrices, harmonised phenotype tables, train/test splits for the random, leave-one-dataset-out and phylogeny-based evaluations, the pruned GTDB tree and distance matrix, KEGG reference mappings, source data for every script-generated main-text and supplementary figure and table, and 105 trained CatBoost checkpoints. items.summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
items.title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

items.summary: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.
items.title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?

items.summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks frame long-term memory as retrieval: can an agent recover the relevant record from a long and evolving history? Scientific agents face a stricter problem: a correctly remembered fact may still be invalid to use. The same reported test result can support confirmation when the outcome and stopping rule were fixed in advance, yet only exploration when the outcome was selected from twenty inspected results. We call this scientific use validity: whether remembered evidence is eligible to influence a decision under the state governing its interpretation. We introduce SciValidityBench, an executable benchmark factory with 64 TaskSpecs spanning five validity modules and six scientific domains. TaskSpecs couple generated experimental histories with scientific-state definitions, programmatic decision oracles, controlled interventions, and automatic scoring. The SciStateForge compiler-reader framework turns distributed histories into explicit decision-governing state. Counterfactual pairs and targeted corruption-repair controls then test whether models use those dependencies and localize failures. Across four model families, compiled scientific state improves valid decision-making by 9.2-18.8 percentage points over a generic Event Graph. Retrieval alone does not reproduce this cross-family gain, while content-identical flat and typed views show that the improvement comes from exposing governing state rather than a particular graph serialization. SciValidityBench thus shifts memory evaluation from finding the right fact to deciding whether that fact should control the decision.
items.title: The Right Fact, the Wrong Decision: SciValidityBench for Scientific Agent Memory

items.summary: Long-horizon agents continually accumulate experience, yet retaining a memory does not guarantee access when it is needed. Existing systems can adapt both memory content and access; we isolate persistent access updates as a separately controlled adaptation layer. We formulate this target as Memory Index Evolution and instantiate it with Adaptive Memory Index Evolution (AMIE), a lightweight plug-in layer that evolves per-memory access state from deployment retrievals without modifying stored content or retraining the host memory system. AMIE distils a semantic teacher's keep/suppress judgments into a retrieval-conditioned policy and accumulates its selective actions into bounded state that reweights subsequent host retrievals. Surprisingly, even a zero-call policy that simply accumulates retrieval frequency can match or outperform semantic policies in several settings, revealing retrieval traffic itself as a strong signal for access adaptation, while learned selectivity improves robustness when frequently retrieved memories remain useful. Across five retrieval-based hosts and three benchmarks, trained AMIE improves downstream F1 or accuracy in all 15 comparisons, by 0.70--3.37 percentage points (up to 25% relative), and improves retrieval in all 10 comparisons. Controlled analyses show that persistent competitor suppression can expose previously unseen evidence, while suppressing repeatedly useful memories creates the complementary failure mode. Together, these results establish persistent memory access as a practical adaptation layer, distinct from the content it serves, in retrieval-based agent memory systems.
items.title: Adaptive Memory Index Evolution for Agents

items.summary: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
items.title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport

items.summary: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
items.title: Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition
